good_form.point: Swing down through the ball from high to low, keeping the racket face square, then let the racket rise after contact.
Turn early and take the racket back high, above the shoulder or head, to create leverage.
Keep the racket face angle fixed through the downward swing, because the face sets direction and height and the path adds spin.
Keep the wrist firm and steady with no change in angle, and let the forearm and big muscles control the face.
Use a Continental (hammer) grip so racket and forearm line up and the face is square to the net at contact.
Play the stroke from the shoulder and back, with little elbow, and relax the arm once the forward swing starts.
Stay side-on and open up only after contact, with the non-hitting arm held back for balance.
Coil past parallel to the baseline with the head steady and eyes on the ball, then uncoil forward into the shot.
Vary depth, height, speed and spin by changing follow-through length, face openness and swing speed.
Contact the ball at your side and slightly further back than a normal backhand, and come down through it, not across it.
Hold the finish and follow-through, and keep the L-shape to control depth.
Keep the racket tip travelling down through contact, in a U-shaped path, to get underspin and bite.
Keep the racket on the same side of the body instead of pulling it across.
Hit mostly flat (about 70%) before adding underspin, so the ball skims low and fast.

faults.description: Using the wrist to flick, drop, snatch or steer the racket so the wrist angle changes.

causes.cause: The small muscles of the wrist steer the racket instead of the big muscles.
The wrist is not held firm.
Taking risky adjustments to the swing.

fixes.idea: Keep the wrist fixed and flat, and lead forward with the knuckles and the bottom of the handle.
Pull with the shoulder and triceps extension and use only small wrist adjustments.
Freeze at the finish to check the wrist angle.

outcome_effects: Inconsistent, unreliable shot.
Less control.
The stroke looks chopped.

faults.description: Using an Eastern, forehand-ish or Eastern backhand grip instead of Continental for the slice.

causes.cause: Amateurs only partly turn the grip toward Continental.
An Eastern backhand grip is used from habit.

fixes.idea: Move to a full Continental grip and check that racket and forearm are in line, for example with the ball-tube test.
Check the grip by holding the racket at head height with a flat wrist.

outcome_effects: Ball floats because the face is too open.
Racket cuts across the ball and adds heavy side spin.
Slices on wide, low or defensive balls are hard to hit, so shot variety is limited.
The face goes very flat when closed.
faults.disagreement: Sources differ on the result: 1 says heavy side spin, 7 says an open face and floating ball, and 11 says an awkward defensive slice and a flat face when closed.

faults.description: The turn is late and the racket stays low and flat, so there is no leverage for a downward swing.

causes.cause: The racket is taken straight back low instead of being lifted.
The player turns too late.

fixes.idea: Turn early and set the racket above the shoulder or head to create leverage, then swing down through the ball.

outcome_effects: The player is too slow and poorly set up when the ball arrives.

faults.description: The body and chest rotate open before contact, with the non-hitting arm left at the side.

causes.cause: The non-hitting arm stays at the side instead of being held back.
The player believes a big rotation adds power or is used to coming around the ball.

fixes.idea: Stay side-on until contact and open up only afterward.
Pull the non-hitting arm back until you feel a squeeze between the shoulder blades.
Face more away from the target in preparation.
Hold the finish like an eagle with the head still, even if it feels jerky.

outcome_effects: Direction is hard to control.
Ball pops up or goes anywhere.
Momentum goes across the ball, so power is lost.

faults.description: The racket goes under the ball with level shoulders or dropped elbow instead of coming down on it from above.

causes.cause: The racket and elbow drop early.
The front shoulder does not tilt toward the ball.
The face is not squared first.
Trajectory is adjusted by going high to low instead of low to high.

fixes.idea: Drop the front shoulder as you lean in so the racket gets behind the ball.
Keep the elbow and racket high, square the face and chop down.
Hit flat first, even into the net, then adjust from low to high.
Aim for about 70% flat and stay on top of the ball.

outcome_effects: Slice pops up and floats.
Ball has little speed and sits up for the opponent.
The slice is too slicy.

faults.description: Tensing the arm and opening the chest to add power instead of using the shoulder and back.

causes.cause: The player starts from a weak, uncoiled position, so the arm supplies the effort.

fixes.idea: Set up in the coiled position, then relax the arm once the forward swing starts.

outcome_effects: The shot has less energy.
The stroke looks strained.

faults.description: Meeting the ball out in front of the body so the racket slides across it.

causes.cause: The grip sits behind the handle and pulls the contact point forward.

fixes.idea: Keep the ball more at your side and come down the ball, not across it.
Slice against a wall and check that the ball comes straight back with no side spin.

outcome_effects: Side spin on the ball.
On a practice wall the ball shoots off to the forehand side.

faults.description: The racket and arm drop out of the L-shape during or at the end of the swing.

fixes.idea: Hold the follow-through and keep the L-shape at the end of the swing.

faults.description: Swinging from the elbow and straightening the racket-arm angle on the way to contact.

causes.cause: Swinging mostly from the elbow and using the wrist.

fixes.idea: Imagine the racket and arm are locked so the angle cannot change.
Play the slice from the shoulder with little elbow.

faults.description: The face angle changes from swing to swing as the racket comes down.

causes.cause: Trouble keeping the face angle as the racket descends.

fixes.idea: Keep the same face angle through the downward path.
Stabilize the racket with a Continental grip and forearm control.
Practise step by step with drop feeds or a ball machine.

outcome_effects: One ball goes well and the next goes off, so the slice feels uncontrollable.

faults.description: The racket face is too open through contact or at the finish.

causes.cause: The setup is not side-on enough, which leaves the face more open than needed.

fixes.idea: Start a bit more side-on.
Feather the racket angle up or down to adjust height.

outcome_effects: Ball pops up too high.

faults.description: After the hit the body turns with the ball and the non-hitting arm is not kept back to counterbalance.

causes.cause: Lack of control over the non-hitting arm after contact.

fixes.idea: Keep the non-dominant arm back to counterbalance the swing, as Federer does, with the head steady.

outcome_effects: Loss of balance and control of the body and shot.

faults.description: Supinating too much, so the racket head is not behind the hand and fights the ball.

causes.cause: Too much supination near contact.

fixes.idea: Find the angle with a little supination, then keep pulling the racket forward through contact.
Practise with no supination first, then add a little.

faults.description: The racket tip whips through the ball soon after contact, like a flat backhand.

causes.cause: Wrist movement brings the tip through after contact.
The whole arm travels horizontally across the ball.
The stroke is approached like a flat backhand.

fixes.idea: Keep the tip toward the outside, then go down and up the other side in a U-shape.
Start high, contact around the waist, keep going down and let the hand rise to non-dominant shoulder level.

outcome_effects: Little or no underspin.
Ball is flattened out and does not stay low after the bounce.

faults.description: Stepping forward to set up, then stepping back during the swing so the body turns away from the shot.

fixes.idea: Rotate forward and turn into the shot as you uncoil.

faults.description: The racket is brought across the body instead of staying on the same side.

fixes.idea: Practise slicing down the line, which keeps the racket on the same side.
Play a down-the-line tram-line point game, scoring only if the slice lands in the tram lines.

faults.description: Hitting completely flat and too much on top of the ball after the flat-first drill.

causes.cause: Overdoing the instruction to hit flat.

fixes.idea: Hit about 70% flat, staying slightly square, and feel the slice.

faults.description: Only a small wrist or forearm movement, with little arm movement through the ball.

causes.cause: Relying on a single wrist or forearm action.
The face is not squared before going under the ball.

fixes.idea: Square the face first, then go under the ball.
Let the forearm rotate through the sequence up, down, then up again.

outcome_effects: Lack of power.
Slice lacks speed and a low skimming flight.

faults.description: The setup is only side-on with the butt cap pointing at the ball, so there is little coil and the racket cuts across the body at once.

causes.cause: The racket is set square behind the ball, so there is no lever to pull against.
The hand and body are not coiled tightly enough.

fixes.idea: Turn past parallel so the butt cap points along the baseline and the shoulder leans toward the ball.
Go from ready position to the coil and hold it, checking it on a screen.
Do shadow swings: pause first, then slow and continuous, then fakes followed by hits.
Rally from the full coil, including while moving along the baseline.
Uncoil forward through the ball first, then let the racket come across.

outcome_effects: Little energy is built before contact.
The racket cuts sideways across the ball.
The player pushes the racket with the forearm.

faults.description: The wrist goes neutral or passive at or before contact instead of staying loaded.

causes.cause: Tension is not held in the grip and wrist through contact.
The wrist is not loaded back in the setup.

fixes.idea: Load the wrists back with the butt cap out to the side.
Hold tension through contact, then let it relax into ulnar deviation.
Grip like a frying pan, not a passive wrist.
Take the racket back a bit higher.

outcome_effects: Racket face opens up.
Slice pops up and floats.
Weak slice with no bite.
faults.disagreement: Source 6 wants a cocked, tensioned wrist, while sources 0, 5 and 7 stress a firm, fixed wrist angle. The sources do not clearly contradict each other.
